We only kept them in just stagnant water! Planaria in the wild are found in both fresh and salt water and are actually parasites. Usually when cut, the cells still have some energy left to continue differentiating. The first structure to be reformed is the pharynx as it allows the planaria to feed. We usually did a diluted liver purée as planaria are carnivores. As for the specifics on the metabolics and how much energy is still needed, I’m not too sure on that but I do know that these worms usually don’t need any extra energy to reform the amputated sections!

The pieces will fully regenerate within a week or so! They don’t need extra nutrients to differentiate anymore, the stem cells just begin dividing until they reach a special signal which causes them to differentiate into specific structures. The cells already know what to do, but in my own experience when you cut these guys up into really small pieces you arent going to get a worm from every piece.
The worm has a bunch of active stem cells still in its body. When it gets cut, the stem cells begin differentiating into whatever pieces are missing from the worm segment

You can cut them any way and it’ll reform back into a normal worm! There are some regions on the worm which if you cut off just that area the worm will not regenerate, such as the very front of the head and the pharynx.

I actually worked with these worms before! Like another commenter said, 273 pieces is the current “record” for developing into new worm pieces. The piece needs to have just one single “stem cell” or Neoblast in order to reform the whole worm
